quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: A proposal to build a tidal lagoon off the west coast promises clean electricity for over a hundred thousand homes. The wall would trap seawater at high tide and release it through turbines. Supporters point out that tides are perfectly predictable, unlike wind. Opponents note that the project would cost several times more than a comparable wind farm and could disturb fish. The government has asked for an independent study before it decides whether to support the scheme.
options: Supporters admit that tides are less predictable than wind, but favour the scheme.
The government approved the lagoon after an independent study confirmed its benefits.
Opponents claim the lagoon would cost less than a wind farm and help fish.
A tidal lagoon offers reliable power, but cost and ecology are disputed.
quests.correctAnswer: A tidal lagoon offers reliable power, but cost and ecology are disputed.
quests.hint: When a paragraph presents a debate, your summary should keep both sides visible.
quests.explanation: Supporters stress predictability and opponents stress cost and environmental risk, with the decision still pending. The wrong options treat the decision as made or reverse each side's claim.
keyPoints: A tidal lagoon could power over a hundred thousand homes.
Supporters value predictable tides, while opponents cite high cost and fish disturbance.
The government wants an independent study before deciding.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: City pigeons are often called pests, but researchers who study them see an animal that has adapted remarkably well. Pigeons find food in places humans overlook, and they navigate using landmarks in ways scientists are still investigating. Councils spend large sums trying to reduce their numbers, usually with limited success. Some experts now suggest that controlling access to food, such as spilled waste, works better than culling. Others say people must first change how they feed the birds.
options: Culling has cut pigeon numbers in most cities, though it costs councils a lot.
Controlling pigeons' food supply works better than culling them.
Pigeons are helpful animals that councils should encourage rather than reduce.
Researchers dislike pigeons because they navigate poorly and find little food.
quests.correctAnswer: Controlling pigeons' food supply works better than culling them.
quests.hint: Separate the researchers' admiration from the management advice.
quests.explanation: After describing the pigeons' adaptability, the paragraph reaches a practical conclusion about food control. The wrong options overpraise the birds, reverse the culling results or deny their skills.
keyPoints: Researchers see pigeons as skilled, adaptable city animals.
Councils have had limited success cutting their numbers.
Experts suggest controlling food access and changing feeding habits.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Doctors warn that antibiotics are prescribed too often for coughs and sore throats, most of which are caused by viruses. Antibiotics do not work against viruses, and each unnecessary course gives bacteria a chance to develop resistance. Resistant infections already cause many thousands of deaths each year. Patients sometimes insist on tablets because they want to feel that something is being done. In response, some clinics now give a leaflet explaining symptoms to watch for, and they offer a delayed prescription that patients use only if they worsen.
options: Antibiotics remain the best treatment for viral coughs and sore throats.
Delayed prescriptions must be used at once by patients who receive one.
Clinics are trying to reduce needless antibiotic use to slow resistance.
Patients now refuse antibiotics because leaflets have explained the risks to them.
quests.correctAnswer: Clinics are trying to reduce needless antibiotic use to slow resistance.
quests.hint: Trace the problem, its danger and the response of the clinics.
quests.explanation: Unnecessary prescriptions encourage resistance, and clinics use leaflets and delayed prescriptions to reduce demand. The wrong options reverse the effectiveness, patient behaviour and use of delayed prescriptions.
keyPoints: Many antibiotics are given for viral illnesses where they do not work.
Unnecessary use helps bacteria become resistant.
Clinics use leaflets and delayed prescriptions to change patients' expectations.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Planting trees by hand is slow and expensive, especially on steep slopes. A start-up has developed drones that fire seed pods into the ground from the air. One team can plant tens of thousands of pods a day, at a fraction of the cost. Critics argue that the survival rate of seedlings is lower than in hand planting, and that the method works poorly in dry soil. Even so, the company insists that speed matters when forests are disappearing quickly.
options: The drones perform best in dry soil on steep slopes.
Drone planting is fast and cheap, and seedling survival is a concern.
Drones plant trees more slowly than human planters.
Critics say drone planting has a higher survival rate than hand planting.
quests.correctAnswer: Drone planting is fast and cheap, and seedling survival is a concern.
quests.hint: Give the advantage and the criticism equal space.
quests.explanation: The method offers speed and low cost while critics question survival and suitability. The wrong options reverse the speed, survival and soil claims.
keyPoints: A start-up uses drones to fire seed pods into the ground.
Teams plant tens of thousands a day cheaply.
Critics worry about survival, but the company stresses speed.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Every time a washing machine runs, it releases thousands of tiny plastic fibres from synthetic clothing. These microplastics pass through treatment plants and end up in rivers and oceans, where fish swallow them. Filters that fit onto the outlet hose can catch a large proportion of the fibres. Some countries are considering laws that would require every new machine to have one. Manufacturers reply that the filters need regular cleaning, which many consumers will forget.
options: Countries have already required a filter in new washing machines.
Manufacturers say filters need little cleaning, so laws would be easy to follow.
Treatment plants remove most microplastic fibres before wastewater reaches the rivers.
Filters could stop washing-machine microplastics, and they need upkeep.
quests.correctAnswer: Filters could stop washing-machine microplastics, and they need upkeep.
quests.hint: Find the problem, the technical fix and the objection.
quests.explanation: The paragraph explains a pollution route, a possible solution and a practical weakness. The wrong options deny the pollution route, reverse maintenance or treat proposals as universal law.
keyPoints: Washing synthetic clothes releases microplastic fibres.
Outlet filters can catch many of them, and laws are being considered.
Manufacturers warn that filters need cleaning that people may forget.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: People who speak two languages often switch between them without noticing. Brain scans show that both languages are active at the same time, so the speaker must constantly suppress the one that is not needed. Bilingual speakers also tend to notice small differences in how people talk. Some researchers believe this daily practice strengthens attention and may delay the symptoms of dementia by a few years. Others caution that many studies have been small, and that bilingual and monolingual groups often differ in education or income as well.
options: Bilingualism has been proven to prevent dementia, according to several studies.
Bilingual speakers use one language at a time in the brain.
Bilingualism may benefit the brain, but the evidence is still debated.
Researchers agree that bilingual studies are large and reliable.
quests.correctAnswer: Bilingualism may benefit the brain, but the evidence is still debated.
quests.hint: Watch for a conclusion that sounds firmer than the researchers' own.
quests.explanation: The paragraph explains a mechanism and possible benefits, then adds methodological doubts. The wrong options reverse the brain finding, claim proof or dismiss the doubts.
keyPoints: Both languages remain active in a bilingual person's brain.
This may strengthen attention and delay dementia symptoms.
Small studies and group differences make the evidence uncertain.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: False stories spread faster online than accurate ones, partly because they are more surprising. Fact-checking organisations try to correct them, but the corrections often reach fewer people than the original claim. Researchers have found that adding a short warning before a post is shared can reduce its spread. Social platforms are testing prompts such as 'Have you read this article?' Early tests suggest that people pause longer when asked a question. Critics say these small nudges will not stop coordinated campaigns, though they may reduce casual sharing.
options: False stories spread slowly online because people find them so surprising.
Small prompts may slow false stories and not organised campaigns.
Warnings have ended the spread of misinformation on social platforms.
Fact-checkers reach more people than the false stories they set out to correct.
quests.correctAnswer: Small prompts may slow false stories and not organised campaigns.
quests.hint: Include what helps and what critics say it cannot do.
quests.explanation: Prompts can reduce casual sharing but not deliberate campaigns. The wrong options reverse the reach of corrections, exaggerate the warnings or reverse the spread.
keyPoints: False stories spread faster than accurate ones.
Corrections reach fewer people, but warning prompts can reduce sharing.
Critics say prompts will not stop coordinated campaigns.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Some school districts have moved to a four-day week to save money on transport and heating. Teachers report that the longer days are tiring, though they appreciate having Fridays free for planning. Parents' views are divided: some enjoy the extra family time, while others struggle to find childcare. Early research suggests that test scores in maths dropped slightly in districts that made the change. The evidence is limited, however, and researchers are waiting for more years of data.
options: Researchers have already reached a final verdict on four-day school weeks.
Four-day weeks raised maths scores in the districts that tried them.
Parents are united in enjoying the extra family time each week.
Four-day school weeks save money and have mixed, still-uncertain effects.
quests.correctAnswer: Four-day school weeks save money and have mixed, still-uncertain effects.
quests.hint: Keep the motive and the uncertain results in one idea.
quests.explanation: The change is motivated by savings, but reactions and results are mixed and the research is unfinished. The wrong options reverse the scores, overstate parental support or claim a settled answer.
keyPoints: Some districts use four-day weeks to save on transport and heating.
Teachers and parents have mixed reactions, and maths scores dipped slightly.
Researchers need more years of data.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Archaeologists excavating a Roman villa welcome volunteers, who make up most of the digging team. Beginners spend their first days learning how to recognise pottery fragments and to record where each item was found. The context of a find matters as much as the object itself, since it shows how people lived. Some volunteers return each year and eventually supervise newcomers. The director admits that progress is slower than with a professional team, but the community involvement brings funding and local support.
options: Professional archaeologists complete the excavation faster, so volunteers are unnecessary.
Volunteers rarely return after their first year at the dig site.
Volunteers slow the dig and bring skills, funding and community support.
Volunteers are not allowed to record where each item was found.
quests.correctAnswer: Volunteers slow the dig and bring skills, funding and community support.
quests.hint: Consider the trade-off the director admits.
quests.explanation: Volunteers reduce speed but add training opportunities and community backing. The wrong options ignore the volunteers' role, forbid recording or contradict those who return.
keyPoints: Volunteers make up most of a Roman villa excavation team.
They learn to identify finds and record their context.
The director accepts slower progress in exchange for funding and local support.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Farm subsidies were introduced to protect food supplies after wartime shortages. Today, critics argue that most payments go to the largest landowners, while small farms receive little. Supporters reply that subsidies keep food prices stable and help farmers survive bad harvests. A recent reform links a portion of the money to environmental practices such as planting hedgerows. Farmers are divided: some see the reform as fair, others as another form-filling burden.
options: Subsidies were created to help farmers plant hedgerows and protect wildlife.
Small farms receive most of the subsidy money, according to critics.
Farmers welcome the new environmental conditions attached to payments.
Farm subsidies are contested, and reforms add environmental conditions.
quests.correctAnswer: Farm subsidies are contested, and reforms add environmental conditions.
quests.hint: Recognise the history, the dispute and the newest development.
quests.explanation: The paragraph traces the origin, current criticism and defence, and the reform. The wrong options change the purpose, reverse the payment distribution or claim unanimous approval.
keyPoints: Subsidies began to secure food supplies after wartime shortages.
Critics say big landowners benefit most, but supporters cite stable prices.
A reform links some payments to environmental practices, and farmers disagree.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Delivery riders for food apps are usually classed as self-employed. That means they receive no sick pay, and many must buy their own insurance. Companies say the arrangement gives riders freedom to choose their hours. Riders, however, report that low pay per delivery forces them to work long shifts, and that turning down orders reduces their future allocation. A court case is now examining whether the riders should count as employees.
options: Riders can reject orders without their future work being affected.
Riders' self-employed status is being challenged over hidden pressure.
Delivery riders receive sick pay and company insurance from the apps.
The court has already ruled that riders count as employees.
quests.correctAnswer: Riders' self-employed status is being challenged over hidden pressure.
quests.hint: Match each side's claim to its own group.
quests.explanation: Companies emphasise freedom, while riders describe pressure and insecurity, and the courts are considering the issue. The wrong options reverse benefits, ignore penalties or treat the case as decided.
keyPoints: Food-app riders are treated as self-employed and lack sick pay.
Companies emphasise freedom, but riders describe pressure to work long hours.
A court is deciding whether they should count as employees.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Hospitals often run out of beds in winter, and patients wait on trolleys in corridors. Managers point to an ageing population and rising illness. Yet analysts find that many beds are occupied by people who are ready to leave but have nowhere to go, because home care or nursing places are unavailable. Building more wards would not solve that problem. Some regions are testing 'step-down' units where patients recover before returning home.
options: Step-down units are already used across the country.
Patients wait on trolleys because they are too ill to move.
Winter bed shortages reflect missing social care, not just missing wards.
Building more wards would quickly solve the winter shortage of beds.
quests.correctAnswer: Winter bed shortages reflect missing social care, not just missing wards.
quests.hint: Look beyond the first explanation the managers give.
quests.explanation: The paragraph shifts the explanation from illness to discharge delays caused by care shortages. The wrong options contradict the claim, reverse the trolley explanation or overstate the pilot schemes.
keyPoints: Hospitals lack beds in winter and use trolleys in corridors.
Many beds are held by patients who cannot leave because care places are missing.
Some regions are trying step-down units.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Language apps reward users with points, streaks and badges. Designers say these game features make daily practice feel enjoyable and keep people returning. However, some learners focus on preserving a streak rather than understanding new words, and they complete easy lessons to protect their score. Teachers point out that real conversation is the best test of progress, which most apps cannot provide. A few apps now include voice chats with tutors to fill that gap.
options: Teachers say apps provide the best test of real progress.
Streaks push learners to study the most difficult material.
Game features motivate learners and cannot replace real conversation.
Language apps already include live chats with human tutors.
quests.correctAnswer: Game features motivate learners and cannot replace real conversation.
quests.hint: Give the app's strength and its limit in the same idea.
quests.explanation: Points and streaks aid habit but may distort effort, and conversation is missing in most apps. The wrong options reverse motivation, teachers' view or the availability of tutor chats.
keyPoints: Apps use points, streaks and badges to encourage daily practice.
Some learners chase streaks by doing easy lessons.
Teachers value real conversation, which some apps now add through tutors.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Public libraries now lend electronic books, but publishers often limit how many times a digital copy can be borrowed before the licence expires. A library may pay several times the price of a paperback for a licence that lasts two years. Readers experience long waiting lists for popular titles that would be immediately available in print. Library associations are lobbying for fairer terms, arguing that lending is a public service. Publishers respond that unrestricted lending would harm author incomes.
options: E-book lending is a dispute over licence terms, costs and fairness.
E-books cost libraries less than paperbacks and can be lent without limit.
Publishers agree that library lending should be unrestricted for popular titles.
Libraries keep their e-books indefinitely once they have bought them.
quests.correctAnswer: E-book lending is a dispute over licence terms, costs and fairness.
quests.hint: Identify the two sides and what each is protecting.
quests.explanation: Libraries want affordable public access, and publishers want to protect author income, so the terms are contested. The wrong options reverse ownership, price and publishers' stance.
keyPoints: Libraries lend e-books under licences with limits.
Digital licences can cost far more than paperbacks and cause waiting lists.
Library groups seek fairer terms, while publishers cite author incomes.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Some cities have begun publishing noise maps that show which streets are loudest at different hours. Residents can check the map before choosing where to live. Planners use the same data to decide where to build barriers or restrict night-time lorries. The maps have also helped to explain why certain neighbourhoods report more stress and sleep problems. Yet critics point out that measurements are averaged, so short, sudden noises may not show up.
options: Planners use the maps to decide where to build noisier streets.
Noise maps show the single loudest street in each city.
Critics say the maps capture sudden noises throughout the day.
Noise maps help residents and planners, and averages hide sudden noises.
quests.correctAnswer: Noise maps help residents and planners, and averages hide sudden noises.
quests.hint: Notice both the uses and the limitation.
quests.explanation: The maps inform housing choices and planning, but they give an averaged picture. The wrong options narrow the content, reverse the use or reverse the criticism.
keyPoints: Cities publish maps showing noise levels through the day.
Residents and planners use them to choose homes and set restrictions.
Averaged readings may miss brief, sudden noises.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Orchards in the valley once grew hundreds of apple varieties, each suited to a particular soil or use. As supermarkets standardised what they sold, most farmers replaced them with the five most popular types. Now a heritage group is collecting cuttings from surviving old trees and grafting them onto new stock. The apples are odd-looking and often bruise easily, so they are unlikely to reach supermarket shelves. The group hopes that farmers' markets and cider makers will create a small but steady demand.
options: The old varieties are easy to transport and store on shelves.
Farmers replaced their apples with vegetables to please shoppers.
Supermarkets are now asking farmers to grow the old varieties again.
A heritage group saves old apple varieties through niche markets.
quests.correctAnswer: A heritage group saves old apple varieties through niche markets.
quests.hint: Follow the loss of variety and the attempt to reverse it.
quests.explanation: Market standardisation reduced variety, and a group is preserving varieties through smaller outlets. The wrong options reverse supermarket demand, the crops replaced or the fruit's durability.
keyPoints: The valley once grew hundreds of apple varieties.
Farmers switched to five popular types to suit supermarkets.
A group is grafting old varieties and hopes markets and cider makers will buy them.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Telemedicine allows patients in remote areas to consult specialists by video. A farmer with a skin problem, for example, can show it to a dermatologist without a six-hour drive. Clinics report fewer missed appointments and quicker treatment. However, video cannot replace a physical examination in many cases, and poor signals sometimes cut calls short. Health workers therefore combine video with occasional visits from travelling specialists.
options: Remote patients still travel six hours to reach a specialist.
Telemedicine brings specialists to remote patients and complements in-person care.
Poor signals rarely affect the quality of video consultations.
Video consultations have replaced physical examinations for most patients.
quests.correctAnswer: Telemedicine brings specialists to remote patients and complements in-person care.
quests.hint: Be sure to include the limits of the technology.
quests.explanation: The technology saves travel and speeds care, and its limits mean in-person visits remain. The wrong options claim replacement, reverse the travel benefit or deny signal problems.
keyPoints: Telemedicine connects remote patients with specialists by video.
It reduces travel, missed appointments and delays.
Examination limits and poor signals mean travelling specialists still visit.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: In a warehouse outside the city, lettuces grow in stacked trays under coloured lights. The vertical farm uses ninety percent less water than a field and needs no pesticides. Because it is close to shops, the produce reaches customers within a day. The drawback is energy, since the lights run constantly and electricity is the largest cost. Operators are therefore locating farms near renewable power, hoping to make the model both greener and more affordable.
options: The largest cost of a vertical farm is transporting its produce.
Vertical farms use more water than field farms but avoid pesticides.
Vertical farms save water and travel, and use much energy.
Operators deliberately place farms far from renewable power sources.
quests.correctAnswer: Vertical farms save water and travel, and use much energy.
quests.hint: Give both the strengths and the drawback that the writer emphasises.
quests.explanation: The farm brings savings and freshness, but its energy demand is a serious weakness that operators are trying to address. The wrong options reverse water use, main cost or location strategy.
keyPoints: Lettuces grow in stacked trays under lights in a warehouse.
The method saves water, avoids pesticides and delivers quickly.
Electricity is the main cost, so farms are moving near renewable power.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: A tax on plastic packaging has been proposed to encourage recycled materials. Under the plan, producers would pay more for packaging made mostly from new plastic. Environmental groups welcome the idea but say the rate is too low to change behaviour. Manufacturers argue that recycled plastic is in short supply and may become more expensive as demand rises. The treasury says it will monitor the effects and adjust the rate if needed.
options: The treasury has fixed the rate and will not adjust it later.
A plastic packaging tax is welcomed, and its rate is disputed.
Environmental groups say the proposed rate is far too high.
Manufacturers say recycled plastic is plentiful and will get cheaper.
quests.correctAnswer: A plastic packaging tax is welcomed, and its rate is disputed.
quests.hint: Recognise that the parties agree on the aim but not on the details.
quests.explanation: The idea is accepted by some groups, but the level of the tax and the supply of recycled plastic are disputed. The wrong options reverse the manufacturers' claim, the treasury's stance and the groups' concern.
keyPoints: A proposed tax would charge more for packaging made from new plastic.
Environmental groups think the rate is too low, and manufacturers worry about supply.
The treasury plans to monitor and adjust the rate.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: A chess club for newly arrived refugees meets weekly at the community centre. Players speak many different languages, but the game needs no translation. Volunteers say the club gives people a place to be competitive and confident when much of their life feels uncertain. Some members have gone on to enter local tournaments, and a few now teach beginners. One organiser observes that the moves are universal, so no one is ever the outsider at the board.
options: Members are prevented from entering tournaments by the club's rules.
The club translates games into several languages for its members.
Volunteers who speak several languages are preferred for the weekly sessions.
A chess club gives refugees confidence and belonging without shared language.
quests.correctAnswer: A chess club gives refugees confidence and belonging without shared language.
quests.hint: Ask what the game provides that words cannot.
quests.explanation: Chess bridges language differences and helps confidence, leading to tournaments and teaching roles. The wrong options add translation, prohibit competition or invent a language requirement.
keyPoints: Refugees meet weekly at a chess club.
The game works without translation and builds confidence.
Some members have joined tournaments or begun teaching beginners.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Many museums hold objects that were taken from other countries during colonial rule. Some governments have formally requested their return, and a few museums have agreed. Supporters of return argue that the objects are central to national identity. Others say that museums can protect and display them to millions of visitors. A compromise gaining ground is long-term loans, under which objects return home but museums retain some involvement in their care.
options: Returning colonial-era objects is contested, and loans are a compromise.
Supporters of return say museums protect the objects best.
Museums have agreed to return the objects they hold, though some resisted.
Governments have stopped asking for their objects to be returned.
quests.correctAnswer: Returning colonial-era objects is contested, and loans are a compromise.
quests.hint: State the dispute and the middle path.
quests.explanation: The paragraph outlines two views and a growing compromise. The wrong options overstate agreement, reverse the requests or swap the two sides' arguments.
keyPoints: Many museums hold objects taken during colonial rule.
Some want them returned as part of national identity, and others stress museum care.
Long-term loans are becoming a compromise.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: A patent gives an inventor the exclusive right to make and sell an invention for twenty years. The idea is to reward creativity, since inventors can recover their costs. Critics argue that patents on medicines can keep prices high and delay cheaper copies. Some countries allow governments to license drugs in emergencies. Economists say the system's balance is delicate, because weaker protection may reduce the incentive to invent, but very strong protection can hurt access.
options: Economists say weaker patents increase the amount of invention.
Governments are not allowed to license medicines, even in emergencies.
Patents reward invention and require a balance with public access.
Patents last for fifty years and prevent copying of the invention.
quests.correctAnswer: Patents reward invention and require a balance with public access.
quests.hint: See the purpose of the system and the concern it raises.
quests.explanation: Patents encourage invention while limiting competition, so the balance matters. The wrong options misstate the duration, economists' view or government power.
keyPoints: A patent gives an inventor exclusive rights for twenty years.
It rewards creativity but can keep medicine prices high.
Economists say the system needs a careful balance.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: In an age of instant messaging, some people have taken up writing letters by hand. They say the slower pace forces them to think about what to say. Recipients often keep the letters for years, which is rare with texts. One writer describes the habit as a way to make a friendship feel more deliberate. But others find handwriting tiring and note that postage costs have risen, so the practice seems likely to remain a small pastime.
options: Some people write letters for their deliberateness, and it will stay niche.
Postage costs have fallen sharply, so letters are cheaper than texts now.
Recipients usually throw handwritten letters away within a few days of reading.
Handwritten letters have now become more popular than instant messages among young people.
quests.correctAnswer: Some people write letters for their deliberateness, and it will stay niche.
quests.hint: Watch the closing prediction.
quests.explanation: The paragraph explains why some people write letters and closes with a limited expectation for the practice. The wrong options reverse popularity, recipients' behaviour or cost trends.
keyPoints: Some people write letters by hand despite instant messaging.
They value the slower pace, and recipients often keep the letters.
Tiredness and postage costs suggest it will remain a small pastime.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Soil stores more carbon than the atmosphere and all the world's forests combined. Ploughing releases some of it, while planting cover crops and reducing tillage helps keep it in the ground. Farmers who adopt such methods often find that soil holds water better and yields become steadier. The transition can be expensive at first, however, because new equipment and knowledge are needed. Some governments now pay farmers for the carbon they store, though measuring it accurately remains difficult.
options: Ploughing increases the carbon stored in soil, so farmers plough more.
Soil-friendly farming stores carbon, and cost and measurement are hurdles.
Governments pay farmers according to precise and reliable carbon measurements.
Soil stores less carbon than the atmosphere and the world's forests do.
quests.correctAnswer: Soil-friendly farming stores carbon, and cost and measurement are hurdles.
quests.hint: Include the benefits and the barriers.
quests.explanation: The practices have environmental and farm benefits but face startup costs and measurement issues. The wrong options reverse the effect of ploughing, overstate measurement or reverse the storage comparison.
keyPoints: Soil holds huge amounts of carbon, some released by ploughing.
Cover crops and reduced tillage keep carbon and improve water holding.
Change is costly, and carbon payments depend on hard measurement.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Amateur weather enthusiasts are contributing to forecasting by linking backyard sensors to a shared network. Each device records temperature, wind and rainfall every few minutes. Meteorologists say the extra data reveals local patterns, such as sudden storms over a single valley, that official stations may miss. Quality is a concern, since poorly placed sensors can produce misleading readings. Researchers are developing tests to identify unreliable stations before their data are used.
options: Meteorologists say backyard data is accurate and needs little checking.
Each sensor records temperature once a day, which limits its value.
Amateur sensors have already replaced official weather stations across the region.
Citizen sensors add local detail if unreliable data is filtered.
quests.correctAnswer: Citizen sensors add local detail if unreliable data is filtered.
quests.hint: Consider the benefit and the condition attached to it.
quests.explanation: Extra data can improve local forecasts if its quality is checked. The wrong options claim replacement, perfect accuracy or infrequent readings.
keyPoints: Backyard sensors feed a shared weather network.
They reveal local patterns that official stations may miss.
Poor placement causes errors, so tests are being developed.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: The old cinema on the corner has stood empty for a decade. Developers want to convert it into flats, arguing that the town needs housing. Residents' groups propose reopening it as a community arts centre with a café and a small cinema screen. Both sides admit that the building's roof needs costly repair. The council has asked each group to present a financial plan, and it has promised to favour proposals that keep the façade intact.
options: Rival cinema plans will be judged on finances and preservation.
The council has already chosen the residents' arts-centre plan.
Developers and residents agree that the building should become flats.
The building is in good condition and needs cheap repairs.
quests.correctAnswer: Rival cinema plans will be judged on finances and preservation.
quests.hint: Keep the two proposals and the council's next step together.
quests.explanation: Two groups have different plans, and the council has set conditions before deciding. The wrong options claim agreement, ignore the repair need or treat a choice as made.
keyPoints: An empty cinema could become flats or a community arts centre.
Both sides acknowledge the costly roof repair.
The council wants financial plans and prefers to keep the façade.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: A flood barrier across the estuary protects thousands of homes, but it is closed only a few times a year. Some residents ask whether the expense is justified. Engineers reply that rising sea levels will make closures more frequent, and that the cost of a single flood would exceed decades of maintenance. Insurers agree, and premiums in the protected area are lower than in comparable places. The barrier's value, in other words, lies in what does not happen.
options: Insurers charge higher premiums inside the protected area than outside it.
The barrier is closed daily to protect homes.
A flood barrier's worth lies in the damage it prevents.
Engineers expect closures to become less frequent as sea levels fall.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: More companies are training employees in mental health first aid. Trainees learn to recognise signs of distress, listen without judgement and guide colleagues towards professional help. They are not expected to give therapy. Participants often say the course makes them more confident about starting difficult conversations. Managers note that people are more willing to admit they are struggling, although the effect depends on whether senior staff visibly take part.
options: Trainees are expected to provide therapy to struggling colleagues in the workplace.
The course makes participants feel less confident in difficult conversations.
Training helps staff support colleagues, especially when leaders take part.
Senior staff involvement has little effect on how open people are.
quests.correctAnswer: Training helps staff support colleagues, especially when leaders take part.
quests.hint: Find the limits of the role and the condition for success.
quests.explanation: The training offers listening and guidance, not therapy, and its impact grows if leaders join in. The wrong options reverse each of those claims.
keyPoints: Employees learn to spot distress and listen without judgement.
They guide colleagues to professional help rather than giving therapy.
Openness improves most when senior staff participate.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Shared kitchens are appearing in cities for people who cook for small businesses. Instead of renting a whole restaurant, a caterer pays for a few hours at a time. The kitchen supplies ovens, refrigeration and cleaning, which lowers start-up costs. Many food entrepreneurs began there, later moving to their own premises. Yet owners note that scheduling conflicts arise when several cooks need the same equipment on busy weekends.
options: Shared kitchens cut start-up costs but can cause scheduling clashes.
Shared kitchens require caterers to rent a whole restaurant for a month.
Weekend demand has little effect on how kitchen equipment is shared.
Entrepreneurs stay in shared kitchens and rarely open premises of their own.
quests.correctAnswer: Shared kitchens cut start-up costs but can cause scheduling clashes.
quests.hint: Include both the value to small businesses and the practical drawback.
quests.explanation: Renting time cuts costs and helps new businesses, but demand peaks create clashes. The wrong options reverse the rental model, the businesses' path or the weekend problem.
keyPoints: Caterers rent time in shared kitchens instead of a whole restaurant.
The kitchens provide equipment and lower start-up costs.
Busy weekends can cause scheduling conflicts.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Microfinance lends small sums to people who cannot obtain bank loans, often women starting tiny businesses. Borrowers form groups that guarantee each other's repayment, so peer pressure replaces collateral. Repayment rates are impressive, and many families have raised their incomes. Nevertheless, studies show that the average effect on poverty is modest, and some borrowers fall into debt when they take several loans. Experts now emphasise that credit works best alongside training and savings services.
options: Borrowers have not fallen into debt through taking multiple loans.
Microfinance helps many borrowers, and its effect is modest.
Studies show that microfinance has ended poverty for most borrowers.
Microfinance requires borrowers to provide valuable property as collateral.
quests.correctAnswer: Microfinance helps many borrowers, and its effect is modest.
quests.hint: Find the hopeful claim and the more cautious research finding.
quests.explanation: Small loans succeed in repayment and income gains, but the overall reduction in poverty is limited and risks exist. The wrong options reverse collateral, the extent of impact and the debt risk.
keyPoints: Microfinance gives small loans to those excluded from banks.
Groups guarantee repayments, and many families gain income.
Studies find modest effects and some debt, so training and savings help.
